title: Pattern Search — Z-Algorithm
directAnswer: To find pattern `p` in text `t`, build the string `s = p + '#' + t` where `#` is a separator that appears in neither. Compute the Z-array of `s` — `z[i]` is the length of the longest substring starting at `i` that matches a prefix of `s`. Wherever `z[i] == m` (the pattern length), the pattern occurs at `i − m − 1` in the text. Building the Z-array is O(n + m) using a sliding `[l, r]` window of the rightmost match.

remember.pattern: Z-function: longest prefix-match starting at each index, computed with a [l,r] window
remember.formula:
z[0] = 0 (by convention); l = r = 0
for i in 1..len-1:
    if i < r: z[i] = min(r - i, z[i - l])   # reuse mirror
    while i + z[i] < len and s[z[i]] == s[i + z[i]]: z[i]++   # extend
    if i + z[i] > r: l = i; r = i + z[i]   # slide window right
rules: Concatenate `p + sep + t` with a **separator that occurs in neither** string, or a long pattern match could spill across the boundary.
`z[i]` compares against the **prefix of the whole concatenation**, which is the pattern — that's why `z[i] == m` signals a hit.
Inside the window (`i < r`) start from the mirror value `z[i-l]`, but **cap it at `r - i`** so you never claim characters past `r` you haven't verified.
Only the explicit `while` extension advances `r`; the window pointer `r` never moves backward, giving the linear bound.
Map a hit back to the text: occurrence index in `t` is `i − (m + 1)` because of the pattern and the one separator character.
whenToUse: Exact pattern matching where you'd consider KMP but prefer prefix-based reasoning
Counting/finding all border lengths or prefix occurrences of a string
Problems framed as 'longest common prefix with the whole string at each position'
antiSignals: You can't pick a safe separator (full byte range used) → use KMP, which needs no separator
Only a yes/no existence check on tiny inputs → built-in find is enough
remember.takeaway: The Z-array answers 'how long does the prefix repeat starting here?' for every position in linear time by reusing earlier comparisons inside a sliding match window. Pattern search is just one read of that array.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can avoid redundant character comparisons using the [l, r] window, and whether you pick a separator that prevents matches from crossing the pattern/text boundary.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Forgetting the separator (so the pattern's prefix bleeds into the text), or not capping the mirrored value at r − i, which over-claims unverified characters.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Explain the mirror reuse precisely — why z[i-l] is a valid starting guess, why it must be capped at r − i, and why r only ever moves right.

problemStatement:
Given a text `t` of length `n` and a pattern `p` of length `m`, return **all starting indices** in `t` where `p` occurs.

Solve it with the Z-function: construct `s = p + '#' + t`, compute the Z-array of `s`, and report every index `i` with `z[i] == m`, mapped back to text coordinates. Overlapping occurrences must all be reported.
constraints: There exists at least one character (the separator `#`) that appears in neither `p` nor `t`
Strings are printable ASCII unless stated otherwise
understanding: The Z-array of a string records, at each index, how far the substring starting there agrees with the string's own prefix. If you make the pattern the prefix of a combined string, a full-length agreement (`z[i] == m`) is exactly a pattern occurrence. The challenge is computing the whole Z-array in linear time instead of O(n·m).

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I assume a separator character exists?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Usually yes for ASCII text. If every byte value is in use, drop the separator idea and use KMP instead — it matches without concatenation.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do overlapping matches count?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — the Z-array naturally reports every index where the prefix-match reaches length m, including overlapping ones.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is z[0] defined?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: By convention z[0] = 0 (or the whole length); we leave it 0 because comparing the prefix with itself is not a useful match signal.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Output indices or count?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Indices in the text. Subtract m + 1 from the Z-array index to convert from combined-string coordinates.

examples.explanation: s = "aabx#aabxaabxcaabxaabxay"; every position whose Z-value hits 4 maps to one of these text indices.
Overlapping matches: in s = "aa#aaaa", three positions reach z == 2.
No Z-value ever reaches m = 1 for character d; empty result.

approaches.name: Naive Z — Recompute Each Prefix Match
approaches.whenToMention: Mention it to define what the Z-array even is before optimizing how you fill it.
hints: For each index i, how long is the common prefix of s and the suffix starting at i? Just compare s[0], s[1], ... against s[i], s[i+1], ... until they differ.
That comparison is up to L characters per index, L = len(s). Doing it independently for every i gives L² work.
Notice you recompute overlapping comparisons many times — that's the redundancy the windowed version removes.
approaches.complexityReasoning: L positions, each comparing up to L characters against the prefix → O(L²) where L = n + m + 1. Space O(L) for the Z-array itself.
approaches.explanation:
The Z-array's definition is direct: for each index `i`, `z[i]` is the length of the longest substring starting at `i` that equals a prefix of the string. The naive build just realizes that definition literally.

**The straightforward loop.** For every `i ≥ 1`, set a counter to 0 and compare `s[counter]` with `s[i + counter]`, incrementing while they're equal and in bounds. Store the final counter as `z[i]`.

**Why it's quadratic.** Consider `s = "aaaa...a"` of length `L`. At `i = 1` you match `L − 1` characters, at `i = 2` you match `L − 2`, and so on. The total is `(L−1) + (L−2) + … ≈ L²/2`. The comparisons at different `i` overlap heavily — you keep re-confirming the same equal characters — and that overlap is exactly what the linear algorithm caches in its `[l, r]` window.

**Why we don't ship it.** With `L` up to ~10⁶, `L²` is 10¹² operations. It's correct and it's a fine way to *explain* the Z-array, but it must be replaced by the windowed build for the size constraints here.
approaches.insight: Naive Z recomputes character matches that an earlier index already proved equal. The whole optimization is to remember the rightmost segment you've already verified and copy results from its mirror position.

pitfalls: Setting z[0] to L and then mistaking it for a match — keep z[0]=0 for search.
Off-by-one in the bound i + k < L causing index errors.
Believing the O(L²) is acceptable at L = 10⁶.

approaches.name: Windowed Z-Function (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Center the explanation on the [l, r] rightmost-match window and the mirror reuse.
hints: Keep a window [l, r] — the substring with the largest right endpoint r that you've already proven equals a prefix of s (so s[l..r] == s[0..r-l]).
If the current index i lies inside that window (i ≤ r), then s[i..r] mirrors s[i-l..r-l], so z[i] is at least min(r - i, z[i - l]) for free — no character comparisons needed.
After seeding z[i] from the mirror, extend it with explicit comparisons only past r. If the match reaches beyond r, slide the window to the new rightmost match.
approaches.complexityReasoning: The explicit comparison loop only ever advances r, and r monotonically increases from 0 to at most L−1. Every character comparison either fails once (ending an extension) or pushes r forward, so the total comparisons are O(L) = O(n + m). The mirror copy is O(1) per index. Space is O(L) for the Z-array.
approaches.explanation:
The windowed Z-function computes the same array as the naive build but reuses prior work through a single sliding interval.

**The window [l, r].** Maintain `[l, r]` as the match interval with the largest right end `r` seen so far, meaning `s[l..r]` equals the prefix `s[0..r-l]`. Initially `l = r = 0`.

**Reusing the mirror.** When processing index `i`, ask: is `i` inside the current window (`i < r`)? If so, position `i` corresponds to mirror position `i - l` near the prefix, and because `s[l..r]` matches the prefix, the Z-value at the mirror `z[i-l]` applies to `i` too — *but only as far as the window extends*. So seed `z[i] = min(r - i, z[i-l])`. The `min` is the crucial cap: beyond `r` you haven't actually verified the characters, so you can't trust the mirror past that point.

**Extending past the window.** After seeding, run the explicit `while` loop: while `s[z[i]] == s[i + z[i]]` and you're in bounds, increment `z[i]`. This compares only characters at or beyond `r`. If the new match `i + z[i]` reaches past the old `r`, you've discovered a farther-right verified segment, so update `l = i`, `r = i + z[i]`.

**Why it's linear.** The only place real character comparisons happen is the extension loop, and every successful comparison increases `r`. Since `r` only moves rightward and never resets, the total number of successful comparisons across the whole run is bounded by `L`. Each index also does at most one failing comparison. That's `O(L)` total.

**From Z-array to matches.** Build `s = p + '#' + t`. For each `i`, if `z[i] == m`, the pattern occurs in the text at index `i − (m + 1)` — subtract the pattern length `m` and the one separator character. Collect those.
approaches.insight: The window is a cache of 'the farthest-right place I've already confirmed matches the prefix'. Inside it, answers come for free from the mirror; only when you'd extend beyond the cache do you spend comparisons — and those comparisons grow the cache, so they're never wasted. That monotonic `r` is the whole linear-time argument.

pitfalls: Dropping the separator — the prefix can match across the pattern/text boundary and over-report.
Forgetting the min(r - i, z[i-l]) cap — claims unverified characters beyond r.
Starting the extension loop from 0 instead of the seeded z[i] — silently O(L²) again.
Letting r decrease — the linear bound depends on r being monotone non-decreasing.

edgeCases.behavior: s = "aa\x01aaaa"; z hits 2 at three text positions → [0,1,2].
No z[i] reaches m → empty result, no crash.
Bug source: choose a byte guaranteed absent (here 0x01) or fall back to KMP.

commonMistakes: Omitting the separator so a partial prefix match spans the pattern/text join.
Not capping the mirror seed at r − i, over-claiming characters past the verified window.
Restarting the extension loop from 0 instead of the seeded value, reintroducing O(L²).

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Missing or unsafe separator
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Without a separator that occurs in neither string, the prefix (pattern) can keep matching into the text and report false occurrences spanning the boundary.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: s = p + t  # pattern's prefix can run into t and over-match
commonMistakesDetailed.good: s = p + "\x01" + t  # 0x01 appears in neither → clean boundary

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Forgetting the min cap on the mirror
commonMistakesDetailed.why: z[i-l] may be larger than the part of the window still ahead of i. Beyond r the characters are unverified, so copying the full mirror value claims matches you never checked.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Extending from 0 instead of the seed
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Re-comparing characters the mirror already guaranteed equal turns the windowed build back into the quadratic naive build.

patternNote: Z-Function prefix matching. Recognise it for any question phrased as 'how long does the prefix repeat starting here?' — pattern search, periodicity, borders, and distinct-prefix counting all read directly off the Z-array.
